utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Joanna Korner, Anna Richterova, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm John Ackerman with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you too. There was sort of an understanding yesterday that we'd start with the witness first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, before we come on to the witness who's here and ready to testify -- and Ms. Richterova is going to deal with him -- there's one matter that arises out of yesterday's testimony from the witness Ms. Sutherland called. Your Honours may recall that he was asked by Ms. Sutherland in chief about how his wife came to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he said he had to sign over the property. Your Honours, what happened was that he said -- he told us that his wife was in possession of documents. They were faxed over yesterday to the Victims and Witnesses Unit. Regrettably they didn't drift up to our office until sometime during the afternoon. A translation was then done, and it's now here. Your Honours, we haven't had a chance to give it to either Mr. Ackerman or to Your Honours, but can we do that. My application would be this afternoon that those documents be entered as evidence subject to, obviously, any objection that Mr. Ackerman may make. I make that application now. Perhaps we can hand out the documents and then deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will hear what Mr. Ackerman has to say after he has obviously seen these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So these documents can be handed --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, they can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Straight away to Mr. Ackerman and to ourselves. Can we proceed with the next witness, Mr. Ackerman? Thank you. Yes. The witness, please, 7.101. Does he enjoy any protective measures? Not that I --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not that I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very soon you will be starting your testimony. You will start giving evidence in this case. But before you can proceed, the rules of this Tribunal require us to ask you -- to request from you to make a solemn declaration, something which is equivalent to an oath, that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of the solemn declaration is contained on the piece of paper that the usher is going to hand to you. And may I ask you to read that declaration aloud, please. And that will be your undertaking with this Tribunal that -- to this Tribunal that in the course of your testimony you will be telling us the truth and the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You may sit down. Thank you. You are Mr. Atif Dzafic, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will be here for a short time. We know that you have already made some statements. And the purpose of your presence here is to give an opportunity to the Defence of Radoslav Brdjanin, who is the accused in this case, to put a series of questions to you. Otherwise, I want you to know that the Chamber, as well as the parties, are aware of the contents of the statements that you have made previously.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are going to be asked some questions by -- is it you, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By the lead counsel for the Defence, Mr. John Ackerman. And it is my duty to explain to you that this is a right that the accused has, to have all witnesses brought forward by the Prosecution cross-examined. The fact that you are going to be asked questions by the Defence doesn't mean that you have a right to put up an opposition to those questions. You have a duty to answer those questions as fully and as accurately as possible and certainly truthfully. So I now leave you in the hands of Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, you know what our decision was on the application of Rule 92 bis. You have a maximum of one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought that Ms. Richterova wanted ten minutes or so before I started my cross-examination to ask this witness some questions. I don't have any objection to her doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's the case, I will certainly allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no objection to her doing that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I had just introductory questions. But because we all have the statements, I just wanted to tender those statements and those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the certification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Okay. Go ahead. It's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Dzafic, just for the record, can you tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Atif Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were born on the 15th of April, 1950 in Sanica in the Kljuc municipality?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You gave to the representative of the Tribunal two statements. One was on the following days, 17th, 19th, and 20th of February, 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And the other one was on the 20th of August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Only the first one with the attachment was certified, and this is the reason I want to tender as evidence -- as -- excuse me, as an exhibit the statement from 17, 19, and 20th of February, 2001, which was certified and was accepted as Rule 92 bis. After your arrival to The Hague, did you have an opportunity to read this statement from 17th, 19th, and 20th of February?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is the content of this statement correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also made yesterday a small correction which were put down by the investigator, and we handed over this supplemental information sheet to the Defence. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So as far as these changes which are in the supplemental information sheet and also in the amendment to your statement, which were certified, and amendments were made on 27th of July, 2001, you can state that everything what you said is correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender the statement and the amendment and the supplemental information sheet as the Prosecution Exhibit P1123.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I do not have more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So Mr. Ackerman, the witness is in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't have a great number of questions to ask you, and we'll try to move through this as rapidly as we can so that you can return home. How many years have you spent of your life as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of September, 1977 -- since the 1st of September, 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you're getting -- you're around 25 years being a police officer of one form or another.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk to you about the structure of the police in Bosnia-Herzegovina right prior to the multi-party elections and how it changed, if any, right after the multi-party elections. The first thing: The structure, the way the police was organised, was all regulated by law, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at the very top of the police structure was the Minister of Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at least after the multi-party elections, the person who held that position was Alija Delimustafic; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber how it would have been under the law that Alija Delimustafic would have gotten that position. How would he have been chosen to have that position as head of -- as Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, after the multi-party elections, the parties that won the highest number of votes agreed amongst themselves which party would appoint the Minister of Internal Affairs. It was the party with the largest number of votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that, in this case, would have been the SDA. And so it would have been up to the SDA party to determine and appoint who would be the Minister of the Interior. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Well, you asked me a moment ago. I told you how long I've been working as a policeman. Then and always we were not allowed to engage in politics, and we were expected to do it ourselves exclusively, to professional police work [As interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that. I think you probably misunderstood my question. My question was only this: After the multi-elections, the post of Minister of the Interior was a post that was determined would be filled by the SDA, that they would appoint whoever it was that would take that post. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And was it an individual that would make that appointment or the main board of the party, or how did that work? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: The appointment would have to be decided by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So if there is a document of appointment of Alija Delimustafic, chances are it's signed by Mr. Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's okay if you don't know. Don't worry about that. Now, in his position as Minister of the Interior, he would have had authority over all of the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is regulated by the law on internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And the next level of authority underneath the Minister of Interior were these CSBs that you talked about, the regional police offices; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: In a specific case, the municipality of Kljuc, we belonged to the regional centre of the security services in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And after the multi-party elections, the chief of the Banja Luka CSB was a gentleman named Stojan Zupljanin; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know who it was that appointed Mr. Zupljanin to that position?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I assume the same minister that appointed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that would have been Mr. Delimustafic?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but I do know that the decision was handed to me appointing me to commander by the inspector from the Republic Secretariat for Internal Affairs in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And who signed your appointment?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. If we go, then, on down to the local police departments, the SJB in Kljuc, that next level at one point at least became the chief of the police -- the chief of the police became a gentleman by the name of Vinko Kondic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know who appointed Vinko Kondic?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I even remember the date when Mr. Vinko Kondic was appointed, because later on he appointed me. It was on the 7th of June, 1991. I was given the decision by the same inspector from the Republican Secretariat of Internal Affairs in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you became -- you continued basically in your position as commander of the uniformed police, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, until the appointment of Mr. Kondic, I also performed the duty of acting chief because it took a long time. We waited for a long time for his appointment to be formalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Once Mr. Kondic was appointed, he then became your superior, your direct superior, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And his direct superior then at that time would have been Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: According to the system of subordination, yes. But the main decisions -- our most important person, the minister, was the one headquartered in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And that would have been Mr. Zupljanin's direct superior, the Minister of the Interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: According to the subordination, the hierarchy goes the centre of the security services in Banja Luka, and then further up Sarajevo. But all decisions and orders that reached us came from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when one became a police officer under the laws of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, one of the things you had to do to be a police officer was to take an oath, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I want to read you an oath and have you tell me if this is basically as you recall the oath that police officers are required to take. "I hereby solemnly declare that I shall perform the duties of authorised officer conscientiously and in good faith, that I shall abide by the constitution and the law and protect to the best of my abilities the constitutional order of the republic, rights, freedoms, and security, and that I shall perform those and other duties of authorised officer even when that means risking my own life." Do you recall that that's essentially the oath that you and other officers were all required to take?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Words to that effect. Yes, that was the solemn oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There came a time -- and sir, please understand when I ask you these following questions that I am not asking you to agree that the establishment of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a legal process. I want to only ask you questions about what happened after that occurred. At some time after the multi-party elections and after Vinko Kondic became -- or at least sometime after the multi-party elections there was a declaration of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which then later became Republika Srpska, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I do not remember the date, but I do know that it was sometime in mid-March that Mr. Vinko Kondic at a meeting in Banja Luka accepted the Kljuc Public Security Station, ranking it among the other 14 or 16 police stations that constituted the SAO Krajina, and he said that from then on we do not have any obligations towards Sarajevo and that we should not act according to their orders and telegrams, and on each document from then on there was the heading that said "The Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." This can be seen from the documents written in those days and while I was still an acting officer, it was required of me to put that in the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so then the police came under the authority of the Minister of Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that point; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: This accession and joining to the centre of security services in Banja Luka and renouncing obedience to Sarajevo was accepted by policemen of Serb ethnicity, whereas the other police officers of non-Serb ethnicity objected and did not accept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to get into that. What I'd like now for you to do is look at an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's a new exhibit. Brdjanin 097, which was handed in just today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'll tell you that the page you have before you comes from the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska and it deals with the police. And the particular paragraph that I'm interested in having you look at is under Article 41, the last paragraph of Article 41. And I'm wondering if you could just tell us what that paragraph is, first of all, and then read it out for us, please.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I think that I didn't provide this in my statement. So in my judgement, there's no need for me to comment on this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, as the Judge told you at the beginning, that you don't get to make those kind of decisions. And I'm asking you to tell us what is that paragraph and then to read it to us, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. Please do as you've been told.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are to answer the question, please. When you've finished reading it to yourself, tell me so that we will proceed with the question. Are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Have you read it, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So the question is: Could you please tell us what in your opinion that paragraph is, what it represents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This paragraph is a well-known paragraph from the law on internal affairs regulating -- that is, the minister defines which persons are considered authorised officers and what their rights and duties are in executing their tasks as police officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The paragraph the question referred to is the last paragraph of Article 41, that is, the paragraph which states "Authorised officers shall take their solemn oath before the minister," et cetera, et cetera. Would you explain to us what that paragraph states.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this last paragraph is the text of the solemn declaration. It is more or less well known to all authorised employees in the police. And before starting employment, each individual is obliged to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And that language is virtually identical to what I read to you a moment ago, which you said was the kind of oath that you would have to take to be a police officer in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, what I did read to you, sir, was the English translation of that paragraph. Now, when the police force came under the control of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, officers were then asked to take this new oath, pledging their allegiance to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, weren't they? And while you're thinking about the answer to that, I'd like the registrar to get Exhibit P140 and show it to you, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I don't know if Your Honours have it, but I can put it on the ELMO so you can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can put it on the ELMO, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, sir, this is -- this is a document which you in fact turned over to the Prosecutor and which you identified as the declaration, the oath, that police officers were asked to take after the Kljuc municipality became part of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And that's what this is, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. But this declaration was preceded by a change of uniforms and insignia and a lot of other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm only asking you about the declaration. This is what I've suggested it is. Do you recognise the name on this declaration?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name on this declaration, the person who actually signed it?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Of course. This is signed by my former deputy. I know his handwriting, and this is his original handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And was he a Serb or a non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Of course he was a Serb. But please, I was -- I am here and it's all -- it's like the final say here. Many things preceded this. This is the declaration, and we all know that. But in practice, it didn't function like that. Let's talk about that. Let's talk about some practical things which preceded this. For example, the change of uniforms, the joining of the Kljuc police to the security services centre, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, we've heard about those things at length over the last several weeks. And the question I'm asking you has to do with this particular document that I've shown you. And it indicates that it wasn't just non-Serb police officers who were asked to sign new oaths, but it was all members of the police that were asked to sign these new solemn declarations, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Look, the signing and also putting on uniforms which had exclusively ethnic insignia was not something that affected police officers who were non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to insist, sir, that you answer my question, and my question is this: All police officers, Serbs and non-Serbs, were asked to sign this new solemn declaration, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, because in the meantime, while pressure was exerted, specifically by my superior on me and other non-Serbs to sign over loyalty to the Serb Republic, at the same time the Republican Secretariat for Internal Affairs in Sarajevo instructed us not to sign these declarations of loyalty because in taking over the duty of the commander, I did not make an oath to the security services centre but I made the oath to the existing government, which at that time was legally elected and which was functioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all -- that's all very clear to us. And these are matters which, as has been pointed out to you, have been explained to us by several of the previous witnesses. However, the question was a very simple one, sir, and I will phrase it myself and hopefully that will bring us to the next question then. I would assume that in the police force before the takeover there were policemen from all ethnicities, from all ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were Serb policemen or policemen of Serb ethnicity, policemen of Croat ethnicity, policemen of Bosniak ethnicity, and possibly also of other ethnicities. My question to you: Were policemen of Serb ethnicity after the takeover asked to make this solemn declaration as well or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were the Croats -- Croat policemen or policemen of Croat ethnicity asked to make this solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And were the Muslim policemen or policemen of Muslim -- not exactly ethnicity, because that's a religion -- of Bosniak ethnicity, were they also -- and you have explained this -- were they also asked to make the solemn declaration, the oath of loyalty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So finally, were there any policemen that were exempted, that were not asked to make this solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there were no police officers who were exempted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has been brought here -- I understood -- Mr. Ackerman gave no reasons for asking him to come here. But all of this was set out on page 13 of his statement. It's absolutely clear. We've spent ten minutes going around the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not true that it was in his statement. He didn't say all police officers were required to take the oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if one looks at page 13 "Reserve policemen from all stations in the municipality of Kljuc were summoned to the respective buildings to sign the oath of loyalty. This included the Serb and non-Serb reserve police officers."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Reserve police officers, yes. I haven't even asked about them yet. I probably won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, sir. Prior to the takeover by the Serbs in the establishment of the government of Republika Srpska, if a person wanted to become a police officer and were handed a solemn declaration for them to sign, and they refused to sign it, could they become a police officer?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. But may I clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: By signing this declaration in a ceremony, this was preceded by three or four important things. Please allow me to state what they are. Following the multi-party elections in Kljuc, the SDS party received the leading place. So Vinko Kondic became the chief, and the commander's post was awarded by the SDA party and that post was given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and has nothing to do with an explanation of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And the points he is mentioning --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the points he is mentioning more or less we know already. Just try to answer the question. This is a simple question. You don't need to worry about the consequences arising out of these questions because those, we have to decide and not you or Mr. Ackerman or Ms. Korner. The question was a very simple one: Would anyone who would refuse to sign such an oath of loyalty expect or be expected to be then recruited as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the present or current conditions, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. That's it. Next question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That solemn declaration that you have there -- that you had there before you. I don't know what you did with it, but you had it there. There it is. Sir, nowhere in there does it pledge any kind of loyalty to the Autonomous Region of Krajina, does it?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Of course it's not mentioned, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to have my original back. I just have one thing to say for the record about it, Your Honour. I want to point out, Your Honour, for the record that the original of this document refers to the law on internal affairs of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Official Gazette number 4 of 23 March 1993. That's what -- now, the original says "1992." The translation says "1993." It's a mistranslated document. All right, sir. The president of the municipality after the multi-party elections was Jovo Banjac; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the vice-president was Omer Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in your statement -- and I'm not going to go through all of these things, because that isn't what you're here for. In your statement you spoke of a lot of changes that were taking place in Kljuc after the multi-party elections and especially as we got up to the early parts of 1992, culminating with that takeover of the police that we've just been talking about on May 7th of 1992. What I -- and that's the way that -- the question I want to ask you: In addition to Jovo Banjac being the president of the municipality, there was a gentleman by the name of Omer Filipovic who was vice-president; correct?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I'd like to ask you is: Why is it that Omer Filipovic did not prevent these things from happening by ordering Kondic, for instance, not to demand this new oath of police? Why didn't he just take over and order that these changes not be made? I mean, he was the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: He was the vice-president, but it is difficult for me to talk about why he didn't do that. I know that he tried on several occasions, according to the ethnic structure, to improve the participation of the Bosniak ethnic group in the police station, so that persons prone to crimes or extremists do not be accepted into police service. So these things really he didn't manage to achieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But as vice-president he had the same authority as Jovo Banjac, the president, didn't he, the same power and authority?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why didn't he exercise that authority and keep these things from happening? That's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know why he didn't. I've already said that he tried to do certain things, but he couldn't do that. It couldn't get past Mr. Vinko. Why he didn't do that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go to another matter. It to refer to some language on page 15 of your statement. It's down near the bottom. It has to do with the death of Dusan Stojakovic. What you say in your statement is that, "I learned that Stojakovic had been killed in Krasulje after Pudin Han and Velagici had been shelled. The people of Krasulje had gathered by the road. Some of them had hunting rifles. A police patrol and about seven to eight members of the manoeuvring unit arrived in the village of Krasulje led by Stojakovic. When he got out of the car, he shot a round of automatic rifle fire towards these people. Somebody from the group of civilians from this village must have returned fire and hit him and killed him." When you say you learned about this, where did you learn about this?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I learned about it in the Manjaca camp, because on the 22nd of May, when I refused to sign this declaration of loyalty that we discussed a little while ago, I went to Sanica with my family because the school year finished one month earlier because my wife, who was the manager of a retail store, was sent on holiday. So I went to Sanica and I was there until the 1st of June, until the Serb police officers and reserve officers pickled me up from my brother's house and took me away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you weren't there, and the only way you know what happened is because of what someone told you.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about this while I was at the Manjaca camp. I knew Dusan Stojakovic very well, while we worked together, before all the problems appeared. We worked very well together. And for a while I was his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just answer my questions when I -- the question was very simple. What you know about this you learned in Manjaca, and you've answered that. The next question I want to ask you about is you mentioned in your statement on page 20 that while you were at Manjaca a man by the name of Vojo Kupresanin came to visit. My question is simple: Do you know what his position was at the time he came and visited Manjaca, what position he held, if any?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I don't know what his position was, but I know that he came because as the person in charge of the barn I was -- the stable, so I was there together with people who were performing the same functions as I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The -- you made a statement of 8 August 1995, and it's a statement that was made to -- it says "Security Services Centre Banja Luka," signed by you and a couple of other people. You're familiar with that statement, I take it? If you need to see it, I can have it given to you so you can see it. I want to be fair with you about what I'm going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I would just like to look at the signature of that statement, and then I can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. I'd like the Prosecutor to give you that statement of 8 August 1995. It's 00488270.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. I gave this statement to a colleague, but I don't know if you are aware that in Travnik there was a Security Services Centre Banja Luka. It had its headquarters in Travnik. After the soldiers came to Kljuc and liberated Kljuc and Sanski Most and so on, they continued to collect such statements, but the heading was still "The Centre for Security Services Banja Luka." But here it doesn't state that this is the Travnik HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're aware of all these things, sir. We've seen other documents like this. I want to refer you to the second page. You're talking about what happened in Manjaca to Omer Filipovic, and there's a paragraph that begins with the language "Three or four days after Omer's conversation by the kitchen." It says "Omer was taken to a solitary cell where he spent 15 days. After the period spent in the solitary cell, Omer was brought back to the barn. He had been beaten up, half alive. They made a calf box in the barn. He was placed in there, and nobody was allowed to come closer to him. He spent one or two nights there, but he was taken for interrogation even in that condition on 27/28, or 28/29 August 1992. After the lights out, a group of policemen came and asked him to come out of the barn." Now, with regard to that, sir, I have just a couple of questions: Were you in the barn -- in that same barn when policemen came and called Omer Filipovic to come out?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't in that barn. That was in barn number 3. I was in barn number 2. But as the person in charge of the barn, in the morning I heard about all of this from my colleague on duty in barn number 3, Zukic, who told me all about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. So again, this is not something you yourself witnessed but something you heard.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I saw a group of police officers when they took him out, because the barns had cracks. We spent seven months there -- almost seven months there. So we could see through the cracks between the planks when they took him away.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I assume you could also hear. Did you hear them call him out?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: I cannot say. I knew that it was Omer, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know Adil Draganovic?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met him at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What barn was he in?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: He was in barn number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You talked in your statement about the visit of Stojan Zupljanin to Manjaca. And at first in your statement you said that he was wearing a blue camouflage uniform. Then when you reviewed that statement on July 27th, 2001, you changed your mind and said he was wearing civilian clothes. Can you tell us why you made that change?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: When I gave the statement for the first time, I wasn't concentrating very well. But since I knew Mr. Zupljanin, I purposely avoided meeting him at Manjaca. And later when I concentrated, then I could see the image -- I remembered exactly where he was, in a suit with a few tie and a white shirt. So it was a civilian shirt, navy blue. There was so much fear in Manjaca, so that when I gave my statement for the first time, perhaps I thought that he was in uniform, because I became used to seeing him in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When did you leave Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of December, 1992, the group before last.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you have a jacket that had been issued to you by the Red Cross, a winter jacket?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you describe that jacket to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: Those winter jackets are well known. Practically all of us got one. It was green and blue here. It was a long time ago. I know that I reached Karlovac in that jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you also were wearing shoes that were issued by the Red Cross, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ATIF DZAFIC
utterances.text: No, not shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Is there re-examination or some questions maybe?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just want to be sure I understand. Is there anything that this witness said in his statement that is actually challenged?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My examination speaks for itself, Your Honour. I won't go beyond it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, there's no re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So Atif Dzafic, that brings us to the end of your testimony here. You're free to leave this courtroom and return to your country, and in fact the usher will escort you out of this courtroom, and then you will be attended to by other officials of this Tribunal, who will make sure you're assisted in your return. Before you leave this courtroom, however, it is my duty and also my wish on behalf of the Tribunal and on behalf of the two Judges that sit with me in this trial to thank you for having accepted to come here and give evidence. Thank you, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to take advantage of the opportunity to thank all those who have invested time and effort and made many sacrifices to prove the truth as to what happened in Bosnia and in Kljuc municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can make -- I'm going to make no comment on the content of the cross-examination, if that's what it was, only to ask this: That in future perhaps reason should be given for why a witness's statement is not accepted under Rule 92. No reason was given -- reasons were given on behalf of General Talic, but no reason was given on behalf of Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't quite agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honour looks at your own decisions on this witness - it's page 4 of the decision --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- and you state: "Brdjanin does not give any reasons -- at paragraph 9: "Brdjanin opposes the admission into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis of this witness's statement unless the witness is required to appear for cross-examination." And then you set out your own ruling that "The Defence should explain the reasons for its objection, having regard to the fact as set out in Rule 92 bis. Brdjanin does not give any reasons for his opposition."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, Your Honour, I had -- I didn't think this witness was even going to be here. I thought I took care of that earlier in the week when I said I had not objected to the Rule 92 bis people, so I couldn't demand that they be here. And when I got a phone call at 4-something yesterday afternoon I was quite surprised that there was an additional witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were not the only one to be surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I thought we had finished with the Kljuc part of this case. So I would hope --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to the rest of our business today. Yes, Ms. Korner, before we do so, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry -- before we do that, the motion that was filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not the motion, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, but I'm sorry, there's something urgent that needs to be done. I was rung by your court deputy and asked whether this motion could be filed openly. The only name that was mentioned in the motion -- that she mentioned was that of Vinko Kondic. And I said no. However, Your Honour, I was unaware of the fact that Mr. Ackerman proceeded to quote a massive chunk from the interview of the witness who is coming, 7.234. Your Honour, that chunk will undoubtedly identify who he is. Your Honour will recall that the witness summons was a confidential one, as far as the matter is concerned, and I am told that by -- when we were informed, the summons had been served, this witness wanted protective measures. So Your Honour, I would ask -- I know it's a bit late, but I only appreciated that when I had a chance to look at it -- but that the motion be not handed to the press section and be filed confidentially now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unless it has already been handed to the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No objection to that, Your Honour. I didn't know these things about this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take your word, Mr. Ackerman. However, we -- Ms. -- Madam Chuqing, do I have an assurance that this motion has not yet been handed to the press, to the public?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. I hope it hasn't. It was only filed at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We will move very fast. We will try to get it back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But it's the decision of this Chamber obviously is in conformity with the requests of the Prosecution as accepted or as not opposed by the Defence. So it will be filed confidential. What I wanted to tell you, Ms. Korner: The document signed by Mrs. Maric, which was faxed to you and which you presented earlier, I suppose is being tendered as an exhibit? In which case, please, could you give us --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next number, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think will be P -- Your Honour, the first one would be P1124. That's the record. I'm sorry, that's the one dated the 4th of August. And then the second one, dated the 30th of October, 1992, would be P1125.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which is the one -- oh, 4th of August. Do you have both, Mr. Ackerman, or do you have one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have them, and I have no objection to them, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So they are so being admitted as P1124 and P1125 respectively. Thank you, Ms. Korner. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Yes. We now come to the motion. And as I take it now, certain points of it will probably require us to go in private session then. No?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, I don't think so. Not for the moment. My concern was that when I saw this chunk -- I say "when I saw it," it was somebody else on the team realised what it would do -- is that that would identify him clearly to anybody reading it. As far as the references to Mr. Kondic are concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay. There's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's no reason, no, why we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Kondic's name has been mentioned throughout this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So it's 3.25. Shall we start straight away or shall we have a short break now and start immediately after? What do you prefer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it your intention to go through this motion today, Your Honour, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because the Prosecution hasn't responded to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but -- I only got it -- it was almost half 12.00 when I was informed of the contents and about 20 minutes later when I first saw it. So I am not surprised at all that the Prosecution have not yet filed a response.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I would expect the Prosecution to make submissions orally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm proposing to. I have one small hesitation, and that's in relation to the first part of this motion, which is that any rulings Your Honour make has an effect on other cases in this building, and that's why I was -- I would prefer to have that dealt with tomorrow after I've had a chance to consult, A, with the Prosecutor, and B, with other people. But Your Honour, I prepared to deal with it this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we'll deal with it. It's a very serious matter, Ms. Korner, as presented.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this Trial Chamber has to look at it, having heard one bell, one bell only for the time being. I think it's our duty to deal with it straight away. We'll certainly listen to what you have to say. And if you need a short time after that to verify things and perhaps then supplement your oral submissions -- your oral argument with further written ones, you will certainly have that opportunity. However, I think we should -- we should take stock of the whole motion today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whether each and every one of these requests being put forward by the Defence will be decided today or not is another matter. But I think we need to hear submissions today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm perfectly prepared to do that. Your Honour, in a sense, I'd prefer to deal with part 2, because that is the more urgent. I hope when Your Honour has heard what I have to say about what in many respects is a misleading account of events given to you on part 1, then Your Honour will feel that that in itself will have no effect on the progress of this trial. But part 2 certainly does, because if Your Honour accedes to Mr. Ackerman's motion, it's effectively -- this trial should be brought to a halt. He's never said it before, but I think he's now saying he can't possibly be ready for Prijedor next week, even with the time off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But even with regard to the first part of the motion, the Rule 68 applicability or alleged violation of, if you see para 32 of the motion, Mr. Ackerman believes that the logical conclusion of his argument, if accepted by this Tribunal -- by this Chamber, should be seizing the presentation of witnesses until this matter is sorted out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's just another -- it's another go, if I may put it that way, at stopping the Prijedor evidence being called at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But let's hear Mr. Ackerman first. Do you prefer to start now or after the break, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think -- I think I have stated my position fairly clearly in the motion. I have tried to. If there are questions that Your Honours have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd be happy to answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We certainly don't have questions. What I was trying to get out of you is whether you want to supplement any further -- these arguments with any further oral submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you're happy with what you have -- and we are incidentally -- I told my assistant legal officer to inform both of you that your request to exceed the usual -- was being granted. So if you're happy with what you have here and feel you don't need to supplement it with any further oral submissions, then we can move to the Defence -- to the Prosecution and see what they --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, as Your Honour knows, I was trying to file it as quickly as I could and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I probably could make it better. So I'm not totally happy with it, but I'm satisfied that it states my position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know what Your Honour -- exceeds the usual what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The page limit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We haven't been given any indication of any page limit because we said we'd reply orally. So I don't know anything about it. The page limit of the motion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, we were told, I think -- I don't think it does exceed the page limit, does it? Twelve pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. Well, Your Honour, I take no point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But anyway, I think it's neither here nor there. It's something that is of marginal or of any -- it's a de minimis, thing anyway. So do you prefer to start now, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm perfectly happy. Whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Would Your Honour like me to deal with it then in the way the motion is set out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest so because I think although all the -- all the matters that -- the items that are discussed here -- and it is indeed three motions in one. But the last two are more or less interrelated. The first one is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it's two motions in one. I don't think there's a third that I'm aware of. The first is the alleged deliberate failure of the Prosecution to disclose Rule 68 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then there is the military one as a result of the severance. And then there is the Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I think military and the Prijedor are wrapped up together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, they are wrapped up, but they are separate too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, those are very simple, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Like Mr. Trbojevic and the rest of the clan. So we'll try to pause between interventions, Ms. Korner and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Because we are committing the same sin that I have been censoring Mr. Trbojevic for.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. Your Honour, the first point I must make, and I have been making it repeatedly over the last few days or the last few weeks, is that I take the gravest possible exception to the constant allegations of deliberate prosecutorial misconduct. Your Honour, there is no foundation for those allegations other than they look good in print. And I deeply deplore the attitude that has been taken in recent times by Mr. Ackerman. Up until now, this trial has been conducted in what I hope is a fairly amicable manner on all sides, and no suggestions have been made on any side of deliberate misconduct. This is now apparently ceasing. Your Honour, this question of the interviews that have been conducted with these persons has been an on-and-off topic since September of last year -- I think last year. And Your Honours may recall that from time to time that the topic has been mentioned, and I cannot now immediately remember in what content I said it or when, but I recall quite clearly telling the Court that the Prosecution was disclosing Rule 68 material from these interviews but was not prepared to hand over the transcripts unless and until, as in the case of the witness that Your Honour knows about, these people were being called as witnesses by us. Your Honour, those are the rules. If the rules are changed, then of course we will abide by them. But Rule 66 says we are obliged to supply to the Defence -- if I turn to -- "disclosure" -- Rule 66: "Disclosure by the Prosecutor." 66(A)(ii): "within the time-limit prescribed by the Trial Chamber or by the Pre-Trial Judge, copies of the statements of all witnesses whom the Prosecutor intends to call to testify at trial and copies of all written statements taken in accordance with Rule 92 bis," et cetera, et cetera. Our only obligation in respect of these interviews is to notify under Rule 68: "The Prosecutor shall, as soon as practicable, disclose to the defence the existence of material known to the Prosecutor which in any way tends to suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt..." Now, Your Honour, I am aware, and indeed we have never for one moment suggested that we should simply tell the Defence that we are in possession of Rule 68 material. We have turned over the nature of that material. Now, Your Honour, this matter did arise in September, as Mr. Ackerman rightly says, at a Status Conference, because it was very shortly after the first series of interviews with these persons had been conducted, and it received a great deal of publicity in Banja Luka. And the matter arose in the way as Mr. Ackerman quotes, save for this: There was a discussion about how the material should be turned over. And in the end the order that Judge Hunt made reads as follows, and I quote from page 357: "Ms. Korner, you've heard what I said." I was -- at that stage -- I should read the previous part. I said: "Until we have the transcripts, we can do no more than indicate that," what the Rule 68 material is. And

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT SAID
utterances.text: "Well, Ms. Korner, you heard what I said. I don't accept that. I expect you to do better than that, to indicate the subject matter of the material, the nature of it, even if you haven't got the precise wording of it. It's your obligation to do it. And whilst if we had another year to wait before the trial started, it would be perfectly appropriate to wait until you've got the transcripts, but this is far more urgent than that and you've just got to cooperate by helping do more than you basically feel you have to." Now, that's, I think, the obligation that we are entitled to insist on both sides but particularly the Prosecution in relation to this material." Your Honour, that was the end of the matter. There was at no stage, contrary to what Mr. Ackerman asserts in paragraph 9 of the motion, that he ordered provision of the actual transcripts at a later date, because at all times since that time we have made it clear we will not provide the transcripts. Now, Your Honour, since that time -- we haven't had an opportunity, because as I say, we got this motion quite late to add up the number of witnesses -- we have disclosed to the Defence from the persons interviewed a bundle of this size, containing not the actual words -- I agree, but a summary of the nature of the -- or in the type that is referred to by Mr. Ackerman. I can hand to Your Honour, because that's been specifically referred to -- to Your Honours -- what we provided. And I accept only on the date mentioned the Rule 68 material from the interview of Mr. Kondic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When -- let me see the document first. And that was handed to the Defence? When.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the date given to Mr. Ackerman. I think two or three days or the beginning of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 15th October; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 15th October. If that's the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Your Honour, on this one occasion, I accept there was a delay. And the reason for that delay -- and I would hope in the light of what Mr. Ackerman knows of me and Your Honours would accept that this was delayed for two reasons: The first is that the investigator who conducted the interview left to go on another mission almost immediately. I was aware that he had been taken off doing -- going through the interview again just before he left because one of the other things we have been doing is conducting a massive, massive Rule 68 search in relation to Prijedor. I think Your Honours have heard this before, that within this building Prijedor is probably the most over-investigated municipality that there ever was. It was the first municipality to be investigated. And the Office of the Prosecutor has accumulated huge quantities of statements, not only taken by the investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor but also submitted by the Bosnians themselves in the original language. Because we were aware of the problems that had been caused in some of the cases that are going to appeal at present, we decided that we would have to do a thorough search not only in relation to the obvious exculpatory material but to see whether witnesses who we were not using had made any statements which contradicted, in a material element, the statements of the witnesses we had chosen to call, because that is an obligation under the Rules. As a result of that, the -- every investigator working was virtually put onto this job, which ran for months. And at the end of that, we have actually disclosed some of the material. I appreciated suddenly that we had never actually completed this exercise in relation to the interview of this man, who was interviewed as a suspect, so that he had a lawyer present. Your Honour, part of the problem arose -- and I make an apology for that simply because of all the events involving General Talic, it just slipped my mind. And remembered it last week and I said that it had to be disclosed. And so on this occasion, I'm sorry, there was late disclosure. And I appreciate that what he has to say is relevant to the municipality of Kljuc. If Your Honour looks at what he's actually saying, we have always erred on the side of, as it were, leniency, because many of the things he says in my view probably aren't Rule 68, but nonetheless we thought it better, as I say, to err on the side of leniency. We have disclosed throughout anything -- and we're going to go back and check through all the interviews to make sure that we haven't missed anything -- that we took could be Rule 68 from these interviews. Not one person, not one witness -- and the Banja Luka people were the first to be interviewed -- has ever been cross-examined on any of the matters that we disclosed. There is a further added aspect to this case. Most of the witnesses - most - a goodly proportion have been seen at one stage or another by the Defence. These are people all available to the Defence living in Banja Luka, all of whose names the Defence are aware of. The witness who is being called, who as I shall explain when we come to calling him, is in a special category of witness, has been seen by Mr. Ackerman's own investigator before we even interviewed him. So Your Honour, we are in the situation where we have not disclosed the word-for-word but the gist or a summary of what was said and what could be said to be constituting Rule 68. Your Honour, Mr. Ackerman's demands, if I go through them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to suggest to you that we take the first part bit by bit as presented by Mr. Ackerman. You've dealt with the Kondic matter. And if you look at para 4, there are two points that are brought up by Mr. Ackerman: First he considers or he submits that there is at least a situation which demands an explanation. And I think you have provided the Chamber with an explanation. And then the second point made by Mr. Ackerman is how could it be that an interview is conducted on 30th August and 1st September and its contents cannot be disclosed until the Defence until 15th October? This is a violation of this as soon as practicable language of 68. You seem, if I read you well, to agree in principle that it is not in conformity with -- what happened was not in conformity with Rule 68, however --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As explained by you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I accept full responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It should have been disclosed earlier and owing to a combination of factors it wasn't. But there was one added factor. And if and if my word is not accepted on this, I will call evidence. The tapes on this interview which was conducted turned out to be extremely bad, and the -- it had to go back to be enhanced and re-recorded before someone could listen to it. But Your Honour, that still doesn't -- only accounts for a small proportion of the time. The majority -- it was my failure. I forgot about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then the next point arises out of what follows. And particularly I refer you, Ms. Korner, to paras 19, 20, 21 in particular, because that's where I fit into the scene. And it seems that there is an allegation that although a year ago more or less -- it's not a year ago, but we're talking of ten months ago -- we had a commitment on the -- on your part that you will be handing -- will be providing the Defence with Rule 68 material with the caveat that you maintained your position that certainly this would not be the full transcripts. Okay? Mr. Ackerman seems to allege, if I read you -- if I don't read you well, please do correct me, Mr. Ackerman. But the allegation as contained in para 23 is that you have not fulfilled this commitment; in other words, that in these ten months, you have not provided the Defence with the Rule 68 material that was in your possession then and which you were working upon. Do I read you well?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I thought I'd dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I want to know whether that allegation -- whether you are accepting that allegation or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're not accepting it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in other words you're saying that whatever Rule 68 material you were working upon way back in January of this year, when all this was entered into the records of this case, has been disclosed to the Defence under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interview -- we disclosed before January of this year, immediately after -- or I can't remember how long after, but we've got a record -- the summaries of what was said which could be considered to be Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not the actual wording. We've never disclosed the actual wording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. I mean -- let's have a break, because I realise that I have overstepped. Let me make the point. If you go back with your memory, as I'm trying to do now, to January of this year. At the time you made the statement, if I remember well, that upon a specific submission or request from Mr. Ackerman, that there were several -- there was probably several material under Rule -- which you would be required to disclose under Rule 68 which you will disclose in due course. But in the meantime, you were still waiting for transcripts of tapes and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll go back in the break and get out the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Check that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The actual transcript for January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That was precisely what we discussed back in January. I do remember it. Take your time. But obviously you need translations and transcripts to be provided before you can actually determine that there is indeed Rule 68 material to be disclosed. So we'll take up the matter from there after the break. We have 25 minutes' break. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I copied for Your Honours the relevant part of the Pre-Trial Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of the 16th of January. Can I hand that in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, I'm sorry. Can I just go back for a moment, while I remember, to the documents that I put in this morning. One of them reveals the whereabouts of the witness. Your Honour, rather than file the document confidentially, could we have leave to redact from the version that we've given to the Registry just the country, and that way it can remain an open document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's how it will be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it's given back to us, we'll give the redaction ourself and then give it back to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the matter was raised by Mr. De Roux at page 496. And Your Honours, you'll see that I say: "We are doing exactly what we were ordered to do last time by Judge Hunt, which is to go through the interviews and disclose in them anything which may be of Rule 68. And that will happen. And it's simply a question of the investigators at the moment re-listening to the tapes. Anything that is Rule 68 will be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Korner please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- December, but in fact I think Your Honour was mistaken there because there was a discussion about Rule 68, but nothing to do with -- I've just checked that-- with the transcripts of these interviews. Your Honour, I've now checked, and of those interviews that were conducted in December of 2001, we disclosed Rule 68 information in relation to one -- I've lost them now. Here we are -- one, two, three, four witnesses. That was disclosed. So I reject Mr. Ackerman's suggestion that we disclosed nothing. And Your Honour, I'm going to come to the question of Mr. Ackerman's memory of disclosure. I don't say he's doing this deliberately but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were there others that were not disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There were others that were read but did not contain Rule 68 material. I mean, others -- I'm sorry, "read" is the wrong way -- that we went through, but there was no Rule 68 material that we could see in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So when you say that you disclosed four, you disclosed the entire.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, we've never disclosed, Your Honour. And I've said this over and over again, and Mr. Ackerman even quotes me saying it in his motion. We have never disclosed the full transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, no. I'm -- leave for the moment -- leave out completely any reference to whether it should be a full transcript --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- or not, because I think that is something which we've heard about enough in the past and which has been dealt with elsewhere as well, and I don't think we need any lectures on that. However, you say: "Your Honour, I've now checked. And out of those interviews that were conducted in December of 2001, we disclosed Rule 68 information in relation to one -- I've lost them now. Here we are -- one, two, three, four witnesses. That was disclosed. So I reject Mr. Ackerman's suggestion that we disclosed nothing." So we disclosed four. Were there any others -- going back to the period December -- September 2001 and December 2001 that should --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- should have been disclosed, or was the four that you disclosed the entire -- in other words, you fulfilled entirely your obligation under Rule 68 when you disclosed those four?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By the -- yes. By that stage, Your Honour, when this was raised we had already, I think, in September or October disclosed Rule 68 information in relation to the first set of interviews. I don't know why I keep calling them witnesses. Persons interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then there was as Mr. De Roux pointed out, it was known that we had interviewed further people in December and we then complied with our Rule 68 obligation in relation to those interviews. Your Honour, I -- in the interval, Ms. Richterova very kindly has gone back and done a check for me, and I should say that interviews were conducted in relation to the Stakic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Before you move to the Stakic case, one moment, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's -- be patient. We -- because there are several allegations, and I don't want to miss any one of them here. There is para 24, which states as follows: "As best as can be determined, what has been provided with regard to the 6 September 2001 order by Judge Hunt are a few notifications of the existence of Rule 68 material. Among these are notifications of interviews with a number of persons that are mentioned here, including an indication of the nature of the Rule 68 material contained in those interviews. In all cases only notifications were supplied. No transcript have been supplied of these interviews." I don't want any submissions on whether transcript should have been supplied. I will then let Mr. Ackerman make submissions on this if he wants to, but for the time being that's not being discussed. And then he says: "The defendant believes and therefore contends that numerous additional interviews have been conducted as to which no material in any form has been supplied." As I read you, Mr. Ackerman, when you say "no material in any form," are you also, because that's the only way it would make sense, suggesting or intimating that not even a notification was supplied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm suggesting is that we have information that as many as 30 or 40 witnesses have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- been interviewed on these summons kind of basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But persons, not necessarily interviews. Persons.
