utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe that to be the case. And the disclosure that was made just last week of Witness 7.242 that they intended to call --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Whatever it is. -- is an absolutely prime example of that. We never knew that that person had been interviewed for three days by the Prosecutor. No information had ever been supplied to us about that, and that had taken place quite some time before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So in other words, basically what you are intimating is that first you believe that there was a substantial number of persons that were interviewed. Secondly, that the interviews might or could contain Rule 68 material; third, that no notification of any 68 material related to these interviews has been made to you; and in addition, no material of any kind has been forthcoming from the Prosecution. This is your contention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was very careful in paragraph 24 to say "as best as can be determined." We made a serious effort to make sure we listed the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But before -- before I put the question to Ms. Korner, I need to read you clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm contesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I will concede that there may be an additional name or two that should have been included here that we missed in our search for the last day of trying to find all of these. But I -- I think we've got them all. I'm not certain of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, can I deal with each of these aspects, Your Honour. Let's deal with paragraph 24 first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A few notifications. Amongst these are notifications of interviews and then there is a list of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Forget those list of names, because it's -- the complaint from Mr. Ackerman is that you've just furnished a notification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. That's untrue. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then explain that. Yeah. Because if he is expecting also the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. He -- if by no he means we didn't supply -- by notification, I understand to mean we simply told him we interviewed these people not true. We provided --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me be very clear before we go further. Can I do that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. We need to clear this up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. By "notification," what I mean is the Prosecutor says we have spoken to this witness and in the things this witness have told us there is the following list of items which we think might be Rule 68. The witness told us things and we think -- our impression is that these 24 items contain within those statements might be Rule 68 material. So we're telling you those items are in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To me that is not a notification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is a notification that there is evidence that contains Rule 68 material. It is not supplying the Rule 68 material because it is not the statement of the witness. It's the statement of the Prosecutor. I'm not -- I don't want the statement of the Prosecutor. I want the statement of the witness. That's the Rule 68 material; not the Prosecutor's statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the problem. It is -- this wild form of allegation, or perhaps it's the use of -- Mr. Ackerman's use of English. Can I show Your Honour: For example, what we -- what is alleged to be notification in the case of Mr. Veljko Kondic, for example. I haven't copied it. I can just show Your Honours for a moment. There are five pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not the exact words of the witness, but as far as we understood, we complied with Judge Hunt's order, which was to give the Defence proper notification -- now, that's different from -- there are two Kondics, Your Honour. One Veljko and one Vinko. And Your Honour, this is my complaint, that all these motions are made public. And each time this type of allegation is made, I have to stand up in public and rebut what is a slur on my professional integrity. And I really do take exception to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So at least we understand now what Mr. Ackerman means by "notifications," which is not what I thought the word would mean, according to my knowledge of that word. But anyway -- so --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the next point I want to know is whether apart from these persons that are listed here in para 24 --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- whether it's true that a further number of persons were interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is so. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As a consequence of which there is 68 -- Rule 68 material that should have been disclosed, and it hasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, there are two matters, Your Honour. The first is we are under no obligation to tell the Defence who else we've interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's another point which --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which Mr. Ackerman is making, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the second is: In respect of the other people that we have interviewed -- and I think -- it's quite difficult to sort of -- the witness that we're about to call, he was interviewed, as Mr. Ackerman -- you see, I'm not sure Your Honours have been supplied yet with the transcripts of interviews --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. On three occasions. And we made the decision at the end that we would disclose the whole set of transcripts, because we proposed to call him. Now, Mr. Ackerman referred to what he asserts and has printed is Rule 68 material. Your Honour, for the life of me I can't see how this can be said to be Rule 68 material, how -- if this is meant to be the part that's italicised -- how it could have been used to cross-examine. If that's what Mr. Ackerman is basing it on, then the answer is no. With this exception, Your Honour -- and that's what I was about to say -- some persons have been interviewed in conditions of confidentiality. I can put it that way? A decision is still being made as to what is to be done with those witnesses. And if there is Rule 68 material in those statements, that hasn't yet been disclosed because we're still trying to work out how to deal with it. But one way or another it will be disclosed. The difficulty is -- is how we do it. But Your Honour, we have that well in mind. And the other exception is this, Your Honour, that interviews were conducted in March of this year in relation to the Stakic case, and those interviews have yet to be gone through before -- we've been disclosing Prijedor Rule 68 or what may be Rule 68 evidence before the evidence starts. So there are some witnesses there that haven't yet been gone through for the purposes of Rule 68 in this case. And Your Honour, if -- and finally on this point, if the Defence -- and of course they are aware, because the whole of Banja Luka knows exactly who is being interviewed, regrettably. Then it's because there was no Rule 68 material contained within those interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is, Ms. Korner -- and we have in one of our previous decisions touched upon this matter and also decided whether it was specifically or it was just obiter dictum I don't remember. But my mind takes me back to a decision which we hand down some months ago related to the applicability of Rule 70, that is, matters which are not subject to disclosure, and I remember quite vividly that we did discuss and decide whether Rule 70, the exemption under Rule 70 covers also material to be disclosed under Rule 98, and we said that -- Rule 68, and we did decide, if I remember well, that the exemption does not apply to Rule 68. Whatever you have, which needs -- which should be disclosed under Rule 68 should be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm well aware of that. I'm not suggesting that if there was Rule 68 and we felt that we were in a position where we couldn't disclose it, we wouldn't be putting it before Your Honour. All I'm saying at the moment is we have yet to make a decision about these people. And I can say that it's not something -- well, I'll have to go back over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if we're talking of persons that were interviewed months ago, if not a year ago, and confidentiality is not an aspect that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're not. We're not talking about anybody that was interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But what's keeping you? Because Rule 68 is -- "The Prosecutor shall, as soon as practicable, disclose to the defence the existence of material known to it, which in any way tends to suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or may affect the credibility of the Prosecution's evidence." Because on the same score, I mean, the -- I'm sure you understand the preoccupation and concern of this Trial Chamber when an allegation is made -- now, whether it's founded or unfounded is another matter. But what we have here are basically two allegations that are very serious allegations. One is that in regard to Kondic, you deliberately took your time to disclose the material, waiting for Mr. Filipovic and Mr. Egrlic, I think, to finish their testimony so that you would be literally taking the carpet from under Mr. Ackerman's feet, disarming him and forcing a situation over which he had no control. The second one is that over the past year or so you have conducted several interviews -- the allegation is -- there's nothing to substantiate this allegation except what is -- what is referred to Witness 7.234, and that -- irrespective of whether that holds water or not. But the allegation is that basing himself on 7.234, he has reason to believe that there are several others that you have interviewed -- several others where there is or should be on your part knowledge of the existence of Rule 68 material, and this has not been disclosed. And this is another serious allegation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And obviously we require some kind of a categoric and unequivocal declaration on the part of the Prosecution that this is not so or that this is so. I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can -- by my count there are three, maybe four, people who have been interviewed and where a decision is pending. And I'm not even sure -- I would have to go back and double-check -- that any of these four people have supplied what could be constituted Rule 68 material. That is something that I can do fairly quickly. I mean, by reading through. Other than that, Your Honour, there is no -- and as I say, there were three people -- four people interviewed in March and relation to the Stakic matter, and those have to be gone through. But those -- there is no problem about -- that -- if there is any Rule 68, that will be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll move to the allegation related to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. And that I utterly refute again, Your Honour, that I deliberately waited for Mr. Egrlic and Mr. Filipovic to finish their evidence. And indeed, I know as well as Mr. Ackerman, that the remedy -- if there is genuinely anything in that which could constitute Rule 68 material on which they could be cross-examined is to have theme brought back again. I don't want that -- Your Honour, if I were deliberately withholding, A, we wouldn't be disclosing this at all; and B --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there was a specific request, in other words --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There was no request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is a forthcoming specific request from Mr. Ackerman for the two witnesses or three witnesses to be brought back here for further cross-examination, you would not object to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Depending on -- I think they would have to satisfy Your Honour that there was really something they couldn't have put before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in principle, you would not object to that as being a remedy if --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- is in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine. That must be right. And Your Honour, I say I am hardly the one, having pointed out how much the cost of keeping -- bringing these witnesses here is to deliberately put the Prosecution in a position where it is obliged to have the witnesses brought back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to 7.234. It's being alleged first that this is a blatant case where there was Rule 68 material that was not disclosed prior to the decision which was taken then to produce this person as a witness. And secondly, the other point made, that this is an example of -- of possibly other cases. Forget that this is possibly an example of other cases, because that has been dealt with other sort of. And do you agree that in the case of Witness 7.234, particularly as regards the part quoted from one of his statements, that there was Rule 68 material that should have been disclosed before by you or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is an example of it. No, I don't. But Your Honour, to be fair, I'd have to go back and have another look at it. The reason that, as I say, I was -- as Your Honours will see, I was present at that last interview and not the earlier interviews. And it became pretty clear to me listening to this that we were going to put this witness -- put this man into the witness box. And so at that stage I waited until the transcript had been typed up so we could then make the application for a witness summons for him. And in all honesty, I have to say that I didn't particularly go through that for Rule 68 material, but I'd have to have another look. I certainly do not consider -- if this is an example of what Mr. Ackerman considers to be Rule 68 material, the part that's quoted, that there was anything. But I have to say, because I was pretty certain we were going to put this man in, I took it in a slightly different category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is an allegation now -- and this you need to do because para 27, Ms. Korner, specifically states that the quotation from the -- one of the statements of this witness - and there were three statements - is being included only for exemplary purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I took it that the best was being picked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. It was being picked -- it's being picked as an example.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the contention is that it is not a complete account of the Rule 68 material contained in his three statements. In other words, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In three interviews. Yeah, okay. All right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour, I have to say here -- because as I say, I ten attend the last of these three interviews, and because at that stage I was pretty certain that he would be put in as a witness, I didn't instruct or go back myself over those to double-check, because we were going to disclose those to the Defence in any event, the whole thing. But Your Honour, to that extent, if there is anything else which Mr. Ackerman regards as Rule 68 material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But I have to go back over it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you go to para 29, Ms. Korner, Mr. Ackerman formulates some demands which, according to him, we should take up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's set out at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But let's take it first here before we go to the end. Because at the end then he modifies the wording and we also come to solemn declarations of some sort or another. In para 29 Mr. Ackerman says: "First we need to order you to advise us who are the witnesses who have been interviewed pursuant to summonses in the Krajina or who in your word were involved in the events." Do you agree that we should do this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't see on what possible basis Mr. Ackerman is entitled to this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Number two: He requests that we order you to identify any portion of the transcripts of any of these interviews that have been provided to the Defence and describe the disclosures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't understand what that means. No portion of any transcript has ever been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, may I ask you to explain this second request in para 29, what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the way it is drafted --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to know if the Prosecutor contends they have ever given us a portion of a transcript of any of these interviews that are the subject of this motion. And she's just told you that she's not and that should satisfy the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's just be clear. We've not -- at no stage, and Mr. Ackerman knows that, have we ever disclosed verbatim transcription of what was said. In each case the form has been, as Your Honours have seen, with the Kondic interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then obviously the third one is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me just say: On occasion I have, with Ms. Richterova and maybe others, said "I don't think I have this document." I get some more information from Ms. Richterova and find that I do have it somewhere. And just as a -- an abundance of caution, I put that in there because maybe the Prosecutor did supply me with a transcript that I've somehow misplaced or something. And so I just want to be certain that there were none.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's simply -- this is not good enough. It is not for counsel -- responsible counsel to make these sort of allegations and then say I'm very sorry, I've discovered that you did give it to me. I'm going to come to that when we deal with the Prijedor part because I have a great deal to say about that. But Your Honour, I have never -- I have always made clear no portion of any transcript verbatim has ever been provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The third one is consecutive and a follow-up, so we don't -- I don't need any explanations about that. May I take you back, Ms. Korner, now to para 10, para 10. Now, there is a suggestion here forthcoming from Mr. Ackerman that the Blaskic decision that he refers to goes beyond what Judge Hunt and myself seemed to have directed you to and that according to Mr. Ackerman, he can now rest on the Blaskic decision and demand transcripts. Do you agree that the Blaskic decision can be read and understood along the lines that Mr. Ackerman is suggesting?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do not, Your Honour. I have the -- I picked up the wrong one -- the Blaskic decision here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the appeal decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is the appeal decision on the 26th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 2000. This related to -- and I think we ought to put it into context. It was in relation to the Kordic/Cerkez evidence, and the application was -- effectively concerned with the disclosure of Rule 68 evidence after the close of the whole case and what the Prosecution's obligation was. And the argument was that the Prosecution was only required to disclose to the Defence existence of evidence. And the ruling was that if the -- the order was, I'm sorry, with -- the Appeals Chamber held that "it was misconceived and that it does not make sense that the Prosecution can stop short of providing exculpatory evidence in its possession, having pointed out to the Defence that it possesses such evidence. If the evidence is in the sole possession of the Prosecution, it is obvious that if the fourth reason were upheld the Defence would be hindered from discovering it, thus frustrating the principle of a fair trial. And the fourth reason cannot stand." And Your Honour, there was no order made in that decision at all, that full transcripts should be provided. Merely that the information in the possession of the Prosecution should be supplied even after the end of the trial. Your Honour, I do not agree that the Prosecution is under any duty to supply to the Defence the full transcripts of these interviews. I do not agree with the demand that the transcript be filed under seal with the Registry in its complete form. Your Honour, we have provided to the Defence the fullest possible notification of what that Rule 68 material is. Your Honour, we say we've complied with our obligations under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It is also being suggested by Mr. Ackerman that the decision of Judge Hunt of the 6 September 2001, as well as the records preceding and also subsequent to that decision, if read properly, mean that you are expected or you were expected by Judge Hunt to go beyond what you have just been maintaining; namely, that basically that at some point or another, after having initially disclosed the existence -- disclosed to the Defence the existence of exculpatory material under Rule 68 without delay, and then you would be expected also to provide the actual transcripts at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, your, I'd be happy if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what is being suggested by Mr. Ackerman, and I will go back to him at a later stage to explain -- to indicate to us the precise parts of the judgement and records.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. If Mr. Ackerman can point to where Judge Hunt ordered us to provide the full transcripts, then I'll be happy to see where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't agree that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to keep repeating this point. Before I finish, over and over again, as I have said when this matter has been raised -- not over and over again. I think it's been raised two or three times since then -- we will provide the Rule 68 material but we will not provide the transcripts. At no stage has Mr. Ackerman or Madam Fauveau, when she was here, sought to argue against that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And last but not last, if you go to para 32, Mr. Ackerman is contending and suggesting that the presentation of witnesses must cease while all this is sorted out, or as he puts it "while it is all sorted out." Do you agree that the presentation of witnesses should cease while this is all sorted out, the Rule 68 business?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So I would stop here with the Prosecution and with the motion for the time being, come back to you, Mr. Ackerman, see what you have to state on this Rule 68 business, and then we'll go -- we'll visit the rest of the motion later. But we'll conclude on Rule 68 first and then we'll visit the rest of the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're free to present your points in whichever order you prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want me to direct you, as I have directed Ms. Korner, paragraph by paragraph, I am prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd actually prefer to do it on my own --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Please do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In my own way, if you'll let me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In your case, I think it would be better if I let you to do it on your own.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to begin with this: Every time that I make any suggestion to this Court that the Prosecutor has not done what the Rules or your order have required her to do, I'm accused of making unwarranted, deliberate, public accusations against the Prosecutor. And if she's getting tired of me making these kinds of requests, I'm getting just as tired of her calling them deliberate, unwarranted accusations. So I'm going to go back. Just a moment. The last time she made that accusation, it had to do with my suggestion to you that it appeared to be virtually deliberate that the list of witnesses from the Prijedor municipality were not provided until what I would consider the very last possible moment. Ms. Korner told you that there was a very good reason for that, and she gave you her explanation after having accused me of making another wild accusation. She said her explanation was that the whole thing of General Talic's situation came up and they had to re-evaluate as to what they would remove from those lists before they gave them to me. If Your Honours will look at the transcript of -- the transcript, page 9342, Ms. Fauveau requested that that material be provided as quickly as possible. Ms. Korner said: "We will have it to you by the end of the week." The end of the week was September 6th. That was the date that she said she would have it to us. That was before anybody knew that General Talic had the condition that he had. It was not supplied then when she said it should have been, and I don't back off from the position I took initially when I raised this. I now take the same position with regard to this Rule 68, and I don't apologise for it, Your Honour, because I am correct. And I will begin this way: At the time this matter was brought to the attention of Judge Hunt, on the 6th of September, 2001, the Blaskic appeal decision of 26 September 2000 had been decided. And if you know Judge Hunt, as I do, he probably virtually had it memorised, knew exactly what it said. And what happened that's of importance to what we're talking about in that case is this: The Prosecution said to the Appeals Chamber, "Even if Rule 68 applies here, Rule 68 doesn't require us to disclose written witness statements, trial transcripts, things of that nature. It only requires we disclose the existence of evidence but does not require the Prosecution to actually provide the Defence with all the evidence in question." That was the Prosecutor's position. The Appeals Chamber said: "The view is misconceived in that it does not make sense that the Prosecution can stop short of providing exculpatory evidence in its position having pointed out to the Defence that it possesses such evidence. If the evidence is in the sole possession of the Prosecution --" which these transcripts I'm talking about are -- "if the evidence is in the sole possession of the Prosecution, it is obvious that if the forth reason were upheld, the Defence would be hindered from discovering it and thus frustrating the principle of a fair trial. The fourth reason cannot stand." That's what the Appeals Chamber said. That's what Judge Hunt had in mind when this hearing was held. Now, if Your Honour looks at this hearing, I had gone through with Judge Hunt that enormous process of all of those CDs that took so much time to get through. And when I stood up and said something about these interviews in Banja Luka, he thought I was going to the same place to get a bunch of irrelevant material that again would have -- be of no -- no use but just take up a bunch of time and maybe even delay the start of the case. That was his original view, and it took me a while to convince him that's not what I was talking about but that I was talking about something else entirely. And that only happened when Ms. Korner decided to explain the situation to him. She said to Judge Hunt: "Mr. Ackerman is aware because it --" and I'm on page 353 "because it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. "That an interviewing team went to Banja Luka with prosecutor summonses. These people who are interviewed are people who are intimately connected with the events in 1992 who have not been charged. No statements were taken. They were interviewed, and the interviews are at present being transcribed. If at the end of those transcriptions -- because a number of people did it, so it's impossible to assess them -- there is material which we consider to be Rule 68 material, then we will decide which of the two courses to adopt. Of course, one is to notify the Defence of the names and addresses of these witnesses. But it appears quite clearly that Mr. Ackerman has already spoken -- I'm sorry. I say witnesses of these people. They are not witnesses at present -- is aware of who they are. Alternatively -- and it depends very much on how we see things -- supply them with copies of the transcripts, but they haven't been typed." That was the first time Judge Hunt really understood what it was we were talking about, and he interjects, "Just a moment, Ms. Korner. You have people within the Prosecution's investigation service who have spoken to these people?" "Yes." "They know what they've said?" "Yes." "And you say there may be things that they've said which may amount to Rule 68 material?" "Yes." "Well, why don't you notify the Defence of that now in some written form and give them the statements later." Those are his words. Ms. Korner then says: "They're not statements. They're interviews." He says: "Or interviews later." In other words, he's saying tell them what's in there, but then give them the interviews later. Ms. Korner then goes on to talk about how they went on for a long time and it's very difficult to pick out from them whether they're Rule 68. And Judge Hunt says: "Look, you said you had a number of investigators. You can ask each investigator was there any Rule 68 material which could be Rule 68 material raised. Have you got any recollection of it? Write it down and notify them and say you will produce the statements later." Again he says "produce the statements later." Ms. Korner says of these people that were interviewed: "I think on balance one could say most of them in some form or another are helpful to the Defence."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you read the previous sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The existence --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, the whole sentence, please. "From if existence of it is these people have been interviewed --"

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I will. "The existence of it is these people have been interviewed, Your Honour. These people are known to the Defence and most -- I think on the balance one could say most of them in some form or another are helpful to the Defence. These are people who were involved in the events." So Ms. Korner characterised --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you read the next sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. "So Your Honour, the Defence to a certain knowledge in one case -- in one case have already interviewed these people," one of them that she knows about. But she's characterised the content of these interviews as helpful to the Defence. Now, that's pure Rule 68. You can't define it any better than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT SAYS
utterances.text: "That's not an answer to your obligation under Rule 68." Ms. Korner says: "It's to notify the existence of Rule 68 material."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT SAYS
utterances.text: "Is that right? Well, if you know of the Rule 68 material. You have to notify them." She says: "Yes." And then Judge Hunt goes on to a kind of a long dissertation about some things and finally he gets down to where Ms. Korner says: "Your Honour, in that case, having heard Your Honour on this --" and I'm on page 357 now -- "we will notify the Defence of the areas which appear to us from these interviews to be of Rule 68 material."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT SAYS
utterances.text: "I don't know what that means. It's what I would call a weasel word. It means what you want it to mean at any particular time. It really doesn't, so far as I can see, comply with Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Your Honour, that's why -- sorry, that's why I said until we have the transcripts, we really can do no more than that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: "Well, Ms. Korner, you've heard what I've said. I don't accept that. I expect you to do better than that, to indicate the subject matter of the material, the nature of it, even if you haven't got the precise wording of it. It's your obligation to do it. And whilst if we had another year to wait before the trial started, it would be perfectly appropriate to wait until you've got transcripts, but this is far more urgent than that and you've just got to cooperate by helping do more than you basically feel you have to do. Now, that's what I think. The obligation that we're entitled to insist of both sides, but particularly the Prosecution, in relation to this material." Now, this was done in the context, Your Honour, of a trial that we were trying to get started rather quickly. And what Judge Hunt was saying to Ms. Korner was you must give him the transcripts, but don't wait until you've gone through them and picked out the Rule 68 material. Have your investigators tell him now what's in there that's Rule 68. And so what she did was the first part. She gave us the little lists of things that she says are -- might be Rule 68 within these interviews but never, ever did she give us the transcripts. I raised it again -- and you will remember this one, Your Honour. This was raised in front of you. And I want to make it clear that I never requested, I don't believe, the full transcripts. All I requested was Rule 68. Although it might be that the full transcripts should be provided under Rule 66, as material important to the preparation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, Rule 66 is conceived on a completely -- a completely different basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. But it might need to be provided under Rule 66, and I'm not waiving that. When I raised it, Your Honour, on 16 January in front of you, you said, "I have quite the vivid recollection of what was stated was that some tapes heard and transcripts made ready and they would be made available. Other tapes were still not heard again and they needed to be heard. And then there was an assurance coming on the part of the Prosecution that whatever falls under Rule 68 would be disclosed." There was then some additional discussion, and then you said to Ms. Korner, "Anyway, I take it as a commitment on your part, Ms. Korner, that anything that needs to be disclosed under Rule 68 will be." Now, I concede that Ms. Korner said, "We will not supply the full transcripts." And by simply saying to you, Your Honour, that they weren't going to supply the full transcripts, left the implication that they were going to supply the redacted transcripts that we'd been talking about from the beginning. And that simply was not done. Now, that puts it in context. That's where we are. And we have this situation now where Ms. Korner is accusing me of making wild accusations, after having had to apologise to Your Honours first today regarding the Kondic matter, for not following Rule 68 with regard to that, and then having told you upon inquiry that there are a great -- that there are many more statements that probably have Rule 68 material that they still haven't gotten through. And so this is clearly not a wild allegation. She's admitted that it has a basis and it has a very sound and significant basis. The evidence -- Rule 68 contemplates the disclosure of evidence. The evidence are the statements made by the witnesses. That's the evidence -- by the persons interviewing. The evidence is not what the Prosecutor says it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rule 68 contemplates disclosure of material.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And that -- the material is material that the Prosecutor has in their position. What she is doing is creating material and supplying it to us. It doesn't refer to material created by the Prosecutor. It has refers to material she has at the present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the word in French? Does anyone have the French text here, please? "Element de preuve" -- "element de preuve," that's the word which is used in the French text, which basically means "material that can be adduced in evidence."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how I could adduce in evidence the impressions by the Prosecutor of what was said by these witnesses. That does not give me anything that is useful. I cannot say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tending to prove, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I cannot say to a witness on cross-examination, "Sir, the Prosecutor says that someone says blah, blah, blah. How do you feel about that?" That's not a -- that would be a ridiculous question to ask in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically it's material as well -- anyway ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, let me talk with regard to the Vinko Kondic matter, which Ms. Korner says she didn't do anything wrong with regard to. It may be that the investigator was gone, and it may be that it was late in the game when that document was able to have been put together, but Ms. Korner knew what Mr. Kondic had said. Ms. Korner knew that Mr. Filipovic and Mr. Egrlic were coming here to testify. On the 30th of July, I believe it was, was when that interview was first conducted -- well, the interview with Kondic was conducted. That was the first day that Mr. Filipovic started his testimony. It went on for quite some time after that -- 30th August. I'm sorry. That was the first day that Mr. Filipovic started his testimony. Ms. Korner was aware of that and did not say to me or to Your Honours "There is material that has been developed which might very well be Rule 68. We probably should wait for calling these witnesses until we can properly provide it to the Defence." She didn't do that. And I think it just amazingly curious that it's only the day that Mr. Egrlic leaves town that that document becomes available and is supplied to us. Now, it may be totally innocent, but it certainly is curious. Ms. Korner seems to be saying that if these are witnesses that we have talked to or can talk to, then she has no obligation to supply Rule 68 material that she might have in her possession regarding these witnesses. No court in the history of the world has ever held anything even remotely close to that. Rule 68 has nothing to do with whether the Defence can on its own discover this material. Rule 68 has to do with exculpatory material in the possession of the Prosecutor. It's like saying, Your Honour, "We have this certified document and there's some language in it which we think might be exculpatory and it says something about a witness so and so," without ever giving us the do you want. You wouldn't permit that to happen. You just wouldn't permit that to happen. And no judge would permit that to happen. And what she's saying to you now is "If I just kind of give them a hint as to what's in these transcripts, that's good enough. I don't have to give them the transcripts." Well, she does. She does. And it couldn't be more clear. The Appeals Chamber has made it clear. Judge Hunt was making it clear when we were talking about it back in September. She says she can't imagine what kind of questions we could have asked on cross-examination if we'd had the Vinko Kondic matter timely. And, you know, I don't know. If I had the transcript, I will bet you I could have done more than an hour of cross-examination just on the transcript of the interview with Vinko Kondic that contains Rule 68 material. I'm not asking for full transcripts. I haven't ever asked for full transcripts. The Prosecution has a right to redact and to only supply those parts of the transcripts that are Rule 68 material. But I question now very seriously whether Ms. Korner knows what Rule 68 material is. She told you today that she couldn't for the life of her, in looking at the quote that I put in here from Witness 7.234, she couldn't for the life of her see what in that quote represented Rule 68 material. Now, if that is the way she makes judgements about what's Rule 68, then when I ask that all these transcripts should be filed under seal with the Registry, that's a request made in very good faith because I want to be able if I have to someday to show an appeals court in this Chamber how much Rule 68 materiel Ms. Korner did not turn over, and I can almost assure you that there will be a great deal of it, if this is her view of what Rule 68 material is. Your Honour sat here and heard in the cross-examination of Mr. Filipovic the contention that there was a coordinated simultaneous attack by Muslim forces across the Krajina on Serb forces, that the Muslims started this process by attacking not just in the Kljuc municipality but in other municipalities all within a space of a very few days. I'm then given, after that's all over, this transcript where a witness from Kljuc says, talking about the 27th, when this killing took place of Dusan Stojakovic: "Prior to that, around 10.00 in the morning, it was observed in the building of the municipal assembly in Kljuc --"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If he's going to read out, I'd like to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I was just going --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I should have said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was just going to suggest that myself. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session again. Mr. Ackerman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There are two things that are exculpatory primarily: The first is evidence that contradicts what the Prosecutor's theory of the case is and indicates that what the Prosecutor is asserting through witnesses and otherwise is not true; the other is evidence that tends to show that the witness is not credible, that deals with credibility of a witness. So that when a witness comes here and says A, B, and C happened, if the Prosecutor has information from other persons that A, B, and C did not happen, that is exculpatory, that is information that affects the credibility of that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is specifically stated in Rule 68 itself, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know it is. I know it is. So I think my requests here are proper. I think they're right. I think they reflect what Judge Hunt ordered and what you obviously understood he ordered, Your Honour, when you spoke about it on January 6th. And I think it's a very serious violation of Rule 68. And I request that Your Honours take the steps that I have suggested in my motion that you take in that regard. And I'll answer any questions you might have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also maintain that the presentation of witnesses must cease while this matter is sorted out, Rule 68 matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's kind of obvious, Your Honour, that that would have to happen, and that's what Judge Hunt told Ms. Korner on 6 September is exactly what would happen if she didn't fulfil her obligations regarding discovery and Rule 68. His exact language was: "If the Prosecution gives you statements too late for you to be able to investigate them properly and which would interfere with the --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "And which would interfere with the proper processes of the trial --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What page are you reading from?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 350. I'm sorry. Bottom of the page. "Then the Prosecution will not be permitted to rely upon them. If they produce material under 68 in the same circumstances, then there will have to be a very long adjournment whilst it's all sorted out." And I think that's where we are. There has to be a long adjournment whilst it's all sorted out. I believe that all of the transcripts of all of these interviews should be deposited with the Registry, that the Prosecutor should be ordered to supply redacted versions of all of those to the Defence as quickly as possible, and then that the Defence should be given a reasonable amount of time to review them and make a report to the Court as to how many witnesses may have to be recalled for additional cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm sorry. I want reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Very short, please, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all -- first of all, that's what I mean about these wild allegations. It is suggested that at the time that I was calling Mr. Filipovic I was aware that Mr. Kondic was giving Rule 68 information. Mr. Ackerman knows that that's impossible because Mr. Kondic wasn't interviewed until the day that I was calling Mr. Filipovic and the day after, when we'd started. I was -- I take full responsibility, because the fact that I didn't know what was in the interview because I wasn't there is not the point. But Mr. Ackerman is deliberately -- suggesting that I knew at the time that he had given an interview Rule 68 material. That is clearly impossible. Because he was interviewed, as Your Honour sees, at the time I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He was interviewed 30th August, 1st September.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I called Mr. Filipovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic came soon after the summer break, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He was the first witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So we started --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 26th, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Exactly. I came back on the 19th and we started on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So Your Honour, that's what I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Mr. Ackerman seemed to emphasise more Mr. Egrlic. The insinuation is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it was quite clear -- Mr. Ackerman said "in the clearest possible terms the time I was calling Mr. Filipovic I knew that Mr. Kondic had given Rule 68 material.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's true. That's absolutely true. Filipovic was here until, what, the 25th of September? Was that the last day he was cross-examined? Was that the last day he left? This guy was interviewed on the 30th of August and she doesn't know by the 25th of September that she's got material from Kondic? I mean, who's running the show in the Prosecutor's office if she isn't? That's the same kind of thing I've been talking about. She give you these weird explanations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The insinuation is there and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel to slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a disgraceful performance. Now, Your Honour, the second matter that I want to deal with is this: We are clearly, and everybody has been at cross-purposes. I understood from the word "transcripts" that Mr. Ackerman was asking for the full transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he is definitely asking for.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And no. He now says he never asked for the full transcripts. Throughout this the discussion has been transcripts or notification of Rule 68. If Mr. Ackerman never wanted the full transcripts but was expecting the redacted version of the transcripts, then I'm sorry, but the ball really was in his court and it's never been raised as to why when he was getting the version that we were giving in the belief, Your Honour, that we were complying with the order that Judge Hunt had made did he never come back to us or indeed to Your Honours and say: "This is the order that Judge Hunt made and the Prosecution are not complying with it." So until today, Your Honour, it's never been my understanding that Mr. Ackerman wanted the redacted or the actual parts of the transcript that dealt with Rule 68. The request was the full transcript, as I understood, and that's what we were declining to give. So Your Honour, I want to make that absolutely clear. And it may be that there's a failure of understanding, although on the face of it we all speak the same language. But I say quite fairly and squarely, if that's what Mr. Ackerman was expecting and wasn't getting it, well, then the remedy was to come back to us and say that or if we still said no, you couldn't have the actual words said, then to raise it with Your Honours. Because Your Honours, as I say, this disclosure has been going on since whenever it was last year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, I can respond really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Please. This will be the end of it and we'll move to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The entire discussion with Judge Hunt on September 6th had to do with Ms. Korner's suggestion that she had to go through the transcripts and redact those portions that were not Rule 68. That's what it was all about. And Judge Hunt said, "Fine. Do that and then supply them. But in the meantime, tell him what is Rule 68 in those transcripts." I never said "Give me the full transcript." And Ms. Korner knows that. And when she said to you on 16 January, "I want to make it absolutely clear we are not going to disclose the full transcripts. We're going to disclose the Rule 68 material," that's what she meant too, that she was going to give us redacted versions. And it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I -- I agree --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the end of it, Ms. Korner. Finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, I really must be allowed. Because it's against me personally these allegations are being made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But he has been making these allegation against you personally from the very beginning. I mean, it's -- the allegations are not being made against --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, why does that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Against --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why does --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- they are being made against you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Why does that make it any better?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't -- yesterday we even had a suggestion that Mr. Trbojevic thanked his colleague of the prostitution instead of his colleague from the Prosecution. But still -- let's leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't follow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's leave it at that. I have taken -- I have taken stock -- note of what you've --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I suggest that Your Honour goes back and reads through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- the full transcript. THE COURT: Of course we will.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And indeed of the December Status Conference, because I think Your Honour was under a misunderstanding. Then Your Honour can see -- and indeed the Judge Hunt conference -- to see the situation. But the situation in any event is left at this, that it's for Your Honours now to rule whether we should supply the actual words used for the -- where we've summarised it. But in any event, Your Honour, that should have no effect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- on the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And one other thing this Chamber is perfectly capable of -- also of distinguishing between malice or maybe an oversight or negligence. I mean, it's -- so I don't think any -- either of you need to worry about the competence of this Tribunal, of this Chamber in deciding these matters. So next. Before I give you the floor on the next matter, Ms. Korner, may I ask Mr. Ackerman to amplify on this. You maintained, Mr. Ackerman, in para 34 that from your client's point of view or standpoint, military documents in this case had been disclosed -- it's as if they have been disclosed to him within the last few days. And then you go on to state that in the Kordic/Cerkez case, a similar situation arose before the Appeals Chamber, and you maintained a significant delay was granted so that counsel could review and digest thousands and thousands of pages of new documentation. Now, I realise that we have not had time to check on this. What was the significant delay that was granted by the Appeals Chamber in the Kordic/Cerkez case?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What I have is -- is not the transcript of what happened, Your Honour, but the report of a lawyer who claims to know, that there was a three-and a half-month delay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how many thousands and thousands of pages are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was told that it might be as much as a million papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Now, Ms. Korner --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can assist. I spoke to counsel involved. It was -- I don't know anything about this. The counsel involved in this, on behalf of whichever accused it was, since the convictions, a significant number of new document collections have been received and the application was in relation to them. Now, Your Honour, I find this part a little surprising. Mr. Ackerman says, "It is as though the military documents were disclosed a few days ago." These documents were disclosed to both counsel at the appropriate time. The fact that Mr. Ackerman took a decision that he wasn't going to trouble to read those documents because they could be left to be dealt with by Talic is negligent. He couldn't know whether those documents were relevant to his client or might be relevant to his client. It is the duty of counsel defending to read the documents supplied, and it is not an excuse to say "I didn't bother because I had Talic's counsel to deal with that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Do you want to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought you had finished on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Because the second part goes with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But forget the second part, the Prijedor, for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no. Sorry. Because -- the problems -- Prijedor are a problem that is equally applicable to this military document side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But I was coming to Prijedor separately, because I prefer to -- because we have tackled both of them already in the past two weeks, not exactly jointly but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but it's linked because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is definitely linked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But this is the next point, I'm afraid. Mr. Brdjanin has chosen to instruct as co-counsel -- or Mr. Ackerman has chosen as co-counsel a gentleman who doesn't, as I understand it, read or understand English, which is a mistake, Your Honour. The languages of the -- the official languages of the Tribunal are English and French. Mr. Ackerman or Mr. Brdjanin must have realised that it was in the interests of him that there should be counsel instructed who was able to read the documents and assist. Now, Your Honour, again, this is a failing on behalf of the Defence -- I mean, how Your Honours are going to deal with it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Neither do we.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's something else. But you know, this is -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, but we are being put -- or the Court is being put in this position because of the way that the Defence has decided to conduct its case. And it is our submission that the Court should not have been -- effectively is being blackmailed on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Ackerman, would you like to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Ms. Korner may very well be correct. She may very well be right that I am negligent for not having read those documents. In hindsight, I virtually agree that I was. If I had any inkling that General Talic was going to develop cancer and the people who had agreed to assume the major lifting on that part of the case were not going to be here, I certainly would have read them. We were -- we were trying to get ready for trial. We were trying to get this case gone to trial on January 23rd, and that was the way we were able to do it, by dividing some of the responsibilities with regard to these matters. That may very well have been a mistake. And if my client is to be punished for my negligence in that regard, then there's nothing I can do about that; so be it. The fact is that there are an enormous number of documents that I simply have not paid a great deal of attention to. With regard to the assignment of counsel, the original rule in this Tribunal was that to be assigned a counsel here, one needed to speak one of the two working languages of the Tribunal. There was a great deal of agitation about that, and the rule was then changed so that a person who speaks neither English nor French but speaks the language of the accused could be named as counsel. But we'd be in no better shape, I suggest to you, if Mr. Trbojevic instead of speaking B/C/S spoke French and not English, which would be one of the working languages of the Tribunal, because he probably wouldn't -- well, we would be in better shape because those transcripts, I think, are available in French. In any event, Your Honours know that I spent the last two or three days working, in addition to writing this motion - which didn't take all that long - but I spent a great deal of time trying to prepare for the Prijedor part of this case. And it became painfully aware that my previous estimates to you of how much I could do in the course of the week are just not right. I just cannot get to where I hoped I could get because the material is just -- tends to be somewhat overwhelming. I'm working at it several hours a day. That's all I can tell you. I've filed my motion. I've said what I need to say. I think I have made my points as clearly as I can possibly make them. I certainly want to ask -- answer any questions Your Honours might have. I have no ulterior motive here other than to try to get my client a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I add one -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I add one thing, Your Honour? I don't understand why they're in this position, because as I pointed out yesterday, the tapes -- or whenever it was, the day before yesterday -- the tapes of -- in B/C/S were delivered in March and April of this year. So can I ask what Mr. Trbojevic has been doing since March/April of this year, or whoever it was. Anyhow, Your Honour, the fact is I don't think there's much I can say, that Mr. Ackerman says he won't be in a position to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What have you been doing, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm glad you think this is funny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been here since June, Your Honour, and I have reviewed the tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is, as I see it, the -- if I am analysing it correctly, I think what is of concern to the Defence at this present moment are two things which are concurrent and which are interacting: It is obvious to me that the Defence is not happy with the decision of the Registry to curtail on the hours that can be recognised for purposes of remuneration; so much so that Mr. Ackerman is saying -- is asking that the Registry should be ordered to suspend our restrictions on Defence counsel and the necessary staff so that these matters will be resolved without significant delay. And that is the first thing that I notice. And secondly, that there seems to be a genuine concern as to the volume of the documents that need to be read, that is, the statements and previous testimonies of the witnesses that -- for part of the Prijedor list. And we discussed this amongst ourselves, between us, earlier on today, and we would like to know roughly what are we talking about? How many pages? What's the documentation like? Is there anyone from the Prosecution that knows?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But I would certainly think it runs into a few thousand pages altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A couple of thousand?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know. Your Honour, one of witnesses has testified in five -- this will be the fifth trial. But that's -- of the witnesses we're starting with, it's fair to say, only one has testified before. They're all new witnesses -- or in the Omarska trial. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first of these witnesses, Ms. Korner, how long do you expect him to be here for?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I haven't got the list, Your Honour. I think about -- I think we estimated two days, because he's a new witness -- or is he? Yes, he is. He's a new witness. So he hasn't actually testified before. Your Honour, I'm -- I'm told something in the region of 2.500 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And do you intend to spread Prijedor evidence to when we break for the Christmas holidays, no? Do you intend to finish Prijedor by --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By Christmas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, that's what our hope is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I just wanted to have a confirmation of that. All right. Do you want to add anything to this, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour knows that I've requested in my motion that -- that you allow me to actually count and tell you how much material it is that I really have to get through, rather than doing this guessing and speculating that I've been doing, and then we'll be able to have a munch better idea. I really believe it's a great deal more than 2500 pages of transcript. That strikes me as a very small number, considering the number of books of stuff I have stacked up on my shelf right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we have dealt with everything. Let's -- how much time have we got left? No, we can conclude now, if I have the indulgence of the interpreters, we can conclude in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So just to make sure that we have covered everything. Your requests, Mr. Ackerman, are the following: First, that the Trial Chamber ordered the Prosecutor to advise the Trial Chamber in writing how and to what extent it has complied with the orders of Judges Hunt and Agius regarding Rule 68 arising from interviews --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please could Your Honour slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- as set out in the transcripts referred to in this motion. That has been covered. B, that the Trial Chamber should order the Prosecutor -- the first one is order but now it's should order the Prosecutor to submit a signed sworn affidavit to certify that she is aware of her continuing obligation under Rules 66 and 68 and has produced to the Defence all material required by the Rules. Do you insist on this, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't really insist on that. I think there has to maybe be a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's being withdrawn, in other words?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. C, that the Trial Chamber determine the additional remedies to be applied for the clear violation of Rule 68. At the minimum the Trial Chamber should order that it be provided be a list of names of all persons -- and we have covered this. Okay. D, after the delivery of the transcripts as contemplated in the previous paragraph, time should be extended to the Defence to review the transcripts and advise the Trial Chamber which witnesses, if any, must be -- okay. We've covered this. E, that the Trial Chamber provide time and direct that the Defence determine the amount of material that needs to be read and processed in order to become familiar with the military aspects of this case. Okay. This, we have covered. And F we have covered as well, that the Trial Chamber provide time and direct that the Defence determine the amount of material that needs to be read and processed in order to become familiar with the Prijedor. Okay. G, that the Registry should be ordered to suspend our restrictions. That, we have taken note of, although it has not been debated. But we also remember the complaint that you raised sometime back, Mr. Ackerman. And finally, that the trial should be indefinitely staid pending the complete resolutions of all these matters. And this has been more or less dealt with as well. In the meantime, we are definitely taking one decision which we are giving orally, and that is that we will resume definitely as planned on the 28th of October and that the first witness that was planned to be brought forward for that week will be brought forward, unless and until this order is countermanded. We will certainly follow up with a written decision, because I think the things being what they are and the allegations being what they have been, I think that it is -- I will discuss it with my -- with my colleagues, because initially I -- I must admit that we had the intention to give -- to hand down an oral decision and leave it at that. But I think matters have become a little bit more convoluted than we had anticipated and I think that having considered what has been stated and alleged here today, we owe it to the trial itself and to both parties to hand down a written -- a written decision. We will work on it as quickly and as efficiently as we can. And it will certainly be handed down before -- well before the 28th October date, when we are supposed to resume.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I've said -- I know I've said this over and over again, but I think Your Honour needs to appreciate a little bit more the difficulty of reorganising witnesses. In my cases the VWS can't just ring them up and say you're on the plane or whatever. They have to be gone and seen because they're not on the telephone and things like that. Therefore, Your Honour, it cannot be left till next week if we're going to have the stop the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But wait -- wait one moment. Because we can't live like this. You know, it's all the time with time limits and deadlines here and deadlines there. Prijedor -- Prijedor municipality. Okay. You have the first one, which is 7.68.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I haven't got a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you follow me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I haven't got a list. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have your list -- do you have -- which I can use? All right. We are going to hand you the list. There is the first witness, which is 7.68.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is shown on the list. Is he or she, so that I don't give a hint, because it's a closed session witness -- is this the first witness that you intend bringing forward or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Correct. So bring that -- prepare to have that brought forward. And that is a witness that according to you you require for two days on chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. I think we estimated two days in all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two days all?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The next one, 7.178.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He will be dealing with Omarska. And as I understand it, is this a witness that has given evidence before? Because it seems viva voce.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is -- this is a witness that has testified before but a long time ago. I don't know whether it's intended to call in full or transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems to me --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The way it put here, it seem that is he's going to be produced in chief and then obviously on cross, as I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- well, Your Honour, it's not quite -- that's not quite the plan. The plan is that yes, his transcript will be used but there may be further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Who -- how many of these witnesses did you plan to have in the first week?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Without the list that I'd prepared, Your Honour, I can't help at the moment. But I think we had, yes, about four -- the first four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Plan to bring those four. In the meantime, we will take -- because the points that have been raised are serious matters. Forget certain points that have been made. But there are certain points that have been made that need to be dealt with thoroughly, especially the Rule 68 business. I don't want the Rule 68 business to delay matters unduly or to complicate matters unduly, and therefore that is a matter that we are going to give attention to immediately. The rest I can tell you does not present major problems to us, so that we -- we could have actually today separated the two issues. But since in Rule 68 there is also a request for the staying of proceedings, we prefer to have everything in one bundle and decide -- decide that very early next week. So prepare to have the first bunch of witnesses to be brought forward as planned the first week of -- not the first week. The week starting the 28th. And if necessary, if necessary, if we come to the conclusion that that cannot be done, then we will make sure that the situation is reversed before it is too late. But we will be working on this motion, giving it our utmost attention, and handing down a written judgement at our first opportunity. All right. I think it is my duty, my obligation, to thank the interpreters, the technicians for your indulgence. We have kept you here beyond -- unduly, but you are also going home earlier. I thank you, and I also thank the rest of the staff. Thank you.
